en: Vāmanadatta:
*Svabodhodayamañjarī*:
Through the investigation of perfect awakening, [one realizes] that mental constructs are devoid of intrinsic nature.
I pay homage to that state of the Self, which has attained the bliss of awakening and compassion. // 1 //
This entire universe consists of nothing more than this group of five, beginning with form;
and it is perceived by the five sense faculties, beginning with the eye. (2)
The eye resides within the minds of embodied beings in all states;
for him in whom that [eye] has dissolved, everything dissolves.
The means for its dissolution was taught by the teachers of old;
out of fear that their tradition might fall into decline, it has been clarified by me. (4)
The conventional usage consisting of the conceptualization of birth and so forth resides in the mind;
however, in reality those [concepts] do not exist. Having ascertained this, one should attain tranquility.
At the time of the union of semen and blood, the mind does not exist anywhere;
it is not in the embryo, nor in the fetal mass, nor is it situated anywhere within the body.
The body—from its dwelling within the womb, through childhood and likewise youth—is momentary, perishing until its end; and yet, it is not truly perceived as such.
Name is separate, form is separate, and the hairs and other parts exist separately;
since everything is seen to be distinct, where then does the body abide? (8)
In this very way, having been examined, the [notion of] genus is likewise sublated;
it is not logically tenable as a real entity, nor does it appear to anyone.
The name given by his father was in vain, since his conduct was not constant;
for if he had been possessed of virtue, many virtues would have arisen.
Having ascertained that the nature of the mind is thus flickering and overwhelmed by the latent impressions arising from false conceptualizations, one should bring it to cessation. (11)
The cessation previously described was attained through the practice of detachment;
this effortless cessation is now taught by us. (12)
Whatever may be an object of apprehension, that too would then be dissolved;
because nothing else is grasped, the mind becomes tranquil within its own self. (13)
Just as when a dense mass of sound gradually dissolves, the mind, by virtue of its dependence upon it, becomes tranquil once that [sound] has ceased. // 14 //
Whatever is captivating that comes within the range of hearing, one should contemplate it with one-pointedness until it becomes absorbed and brings about cessation. 15.
In this very way, one should contemplate the loveliness of form and the other [sensory objects];
afterwards, strengthened by the state of the self, one should remember them as having dissolved away. (16)
Thus, the cessation resulting from absorption into the object has been described by me; now, this former [cessation] arising from the subject itself is being demonstrated. (17)

One should awaken [the practitioner] to the fact that the sense-faculties (indriya) are equal here in their grasping; equality arises from the abandonment of passion (rāga) and likewise from the complete destruction of hatred (dveṣa). // 18 //
From all passion there would be fear, and likewise from all hatred;
one who possesses all passion would be as if bound, and one who hates all would be terrifying.
The sense faculty, ungraspable and empty, dissolves into its own self;
when the activity of the senses has dissolved, there arises the emergence of absolute liberation.

Therefore, by taking hold of the mind within that which is empty and devoid of conceptual construction, the cessation [of thought] arises for one whose sensory activities have become motionless. // 21 //
For a yogin who is constantly yawning, overcome by hunger,
or meditating on something within, there will arise at the very end only [the realization of] the ultimate.
For one whose mental fluctuations have not yet dissolved who gradually resorts to sleep, a complete cessation [of mental activity] arises due to the non-perception of objects. // 23 //
Because one does not perceive the effort involved in the placement of footsteps while running,
and because the activity of the mind is free from volitional thought, the Supreme Self shines forth.
"Even while seated upon a cushion, where does my mind abide?"—by investigating thus with effort, it comes to rest in the supportless state. (25)
I perform the movements of the body, such as breathing and so forth; yet the wind does not reside in the mind, nor does the mind abide in the wind. (26)
For one who reflects thus upon all things, the mind does not abide anywhere; its mental fluctuations are merely mutual, and it remains entirely in a state of absolute stillness.
Wherever there may be a desire for objects such as food and the like, one should fulfill it according to one's ability; thus one becomes complete and independent. // 28 //
If something desired has been spoken and is suddenly forgotten, by reconnecting with it once more, one shall attain liberation in an instant. (29)
When an object seen from a distance is conceptualized as "it might be a post" or "it might be a person," cessation quickly arises for one whose mind is well-ascertained.
Since one perceives the seer through the intellect by means of visible objects, having seen that [seer], one attains liberation; he who does not see in that way is bound.
Having diligently focused upon consciousness, one finds that there is no object of cognition existing by way of its own nature;
therefore, since everything is known [only] through consciousness, one should become composed of consciousness itself. // 32 //
One should enter again by means of the apāna and expand the heart;
in that very way, when the apāna has dissolved, one's mental activity becomes attenuated.
By resorting to the path of the *suṣumṇā* and awakening to the resonance of the *prāsāda*, through the abandonment of the six *bindus*, tranquil awareness arises in an instant. (34)
Through the friction of the two drops resulting from the movement of the left and right [channels],
great peace at the "end of the twelve" is declared by the Siddhas in the Oral Tradition (Mukhāgama).
When the upward-moving breath has reached its limit and subsides, there is likewise the dissolution of the mind upon the breaking apart of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). 36.
Having opened the mouth and remained for a moment without doubt and without agitation, the cessation [of thought] arises for one whose vital breaths have been paralyzed. (37)
At the conclusion of sexual union, one should direct the mind to the space between the navel and the genitals;
while the bliss of passion dissolves, one should remain for a moment free from mental waves.
The mind, filled with joy from embracing friends and kinsmen who have come from afar, attains tranquility in an instant. (39)
Because the meaning of a word is not ascertained when it is uttered from a distance, that knowledge arises for one who is attentive once the obstruction has been diminished. [...
From massaging the feet and embracing, the obstruction of the mind may last for a moment. (41)

Establish yourself at the very tip of the subtle movement of those things that please the palate, such as the six flavors and so forth; when the bliss of rasa is being dissolved away, absolute liberation arises.
In the same way, one should contemplate the fragrances in jasmine and other flowers;
when those [fragrances] have dissolved, the mind dissolves by virtue of having them as its support. (43)
Thus, he whose mind dissolves into the Self at every moment, having attained the true nature of awakening, is called one liberated while living. (44)
This *Svabodhodayamañjarī* was composed by Vāmanadatta, the son of Harṣadatta, that lion among the Mīmāṃsakas. (45)
